summary: This chapter is about understanding what a passage actually says. You will find the main idea, pick out the details that support it, and decide what the passage suggests without saying it directly. It is one of the largest parts of the Reading test, so steady practice here pays off.

Start with the main idea. It is the one point the whole passage is built around, so it should cover every paragraph, not just one example. Next come supporting details, which are the facts, examples, and reasons the author uses to back up that main point.

Inference questions ask what the author implies or what the passage suggests. A good inference is a small, safe step from the words on the page. If an answer needs your own opinion or outside knowledge to work, it is probably a trap.

concepts.definition: The central point of the whole passage. Every paragraph should connect back to it. It is broader than any single example but not so broad that it goes beyond the passage.
concepts.tip: Ask: "Could this be the title?" If it only fits one paragraph, it is a detail.

concepts.definition: A fact, example, statistic, or reason that helps prove or explain the main idea. Details answer questions like who, what, when, where, and why.
concepts.tip: Details hold up the main idea like legs hold up a table.

concepts.definition: A conclusion the reader draws from clues in the text. The passage does not say it directly, but the words clearly point to it.
concepts.tip: Text clues + careful thinking = inference. No clue in the text, no inference.

concepts.definition: Wrong main-idea choices often cover much more than the passage discusses (too broad) or only one detail from it (too narrow).
concepts.tip: Pick the answer that fits the passage like a well-sized coat.

concepts.definition: Correct answers usually restate the passage in new words. Choices that copy exact phrases but change the meaning are common traps.
concepts.tip: Same meaning, different words is good. Same words, different meaning is a trap.

points: The main idea covers the whole passage, not just one detail.
An inference must be supported by the text, not by outside opinions or knowledge.
Watch for questions that ask what the author implies or what the passage suggests.
Reject answer choices that are true in real life but not stated or supported in the passage.

summary: This chapter looks at how a passage is written, not only what it says. You will judge the author's purpose and tone, see how the passage is organized, work out word meanings from context, and tell facts apart from opinions.

Purpose is why the author wrote the passage, such as to inform, to persuade, or to describe. Tone is the author's attitude, which shows through word choice. Organization is the pattern the ideas follow, and transition words are the signposts that show it.

For vocabulary questions, the sentences around the word are your best tool, because a common word can have an unusual meaning in a specific passage. For fact and opinion questions, ask whether the statement could be checked. A fact can be proven; an opinion is a belief or judgment.

concepts.definition: The reason the author wrote the text, such as to inform, to persuade, to explain, or to entertain. A passage may have a main purpose and smaller ones for each paragraph.
concepts.tip: Look at the verbs in the answer choices: argue, describe, compare, criticize.

concepts.definition: The author's attitude toward the topic, shown through word choice. Tone can be neutral, approving, critical, doubtful, hopeful, and so on.
concepts.tip: Find the loaded words; they reveal the attitude.

concepts.definition: The meaning a word has in the specific sentence where it appears. Use nearby words, examples, contrasts, and definitions to figure it out.
concepts.tip: Swap each answer choice into the sentence and see which one keeps the meaning.

concepts.definition: A fact can be checked and proven true or false. An opinion expresses a belief, feeling, or judgment and often uses words like best, should, or unfortunately.
concepts.tip: Can you look it up or measure it? Then it is a fact.

concepts.definition: Common ways to arrange ideas: cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, chronological order, and claim with support.
concepts.tip: Name the pattern first, then answer structure questions.

concepts.definition: Words that show how ideas connect. However and but show contrast; therefore and as a result show cause and effect; for example shows illustration; also and in addition show addition.
concepts.tip: Transitions are road signs telling you which way the ideas turn.

points: Use the sentences around a word to find its meaning in context.
A fact can be checked; an opinion states a belief or judgment.
Transition words show how ideas are related.
Tone comes from word choice, so look for words with strong positive or negative feelings.
The most common meaning of a word is often not the answer in vocabulary-in-context questions.

compare.title: Purpose vs. tone
rows: Why did the author write this?
How does the author feel about it?

summary: This chapter asks you to connect and judge information. You will read charts and graphs alongside text, decide whether an argument's evidence holds up, and compare two passages on the same topic. It carries as much weight as the Key Ideas chapter.

With charts and graphs, read the title, labels, and units before looking at the numbers. Then check whether the text and the graphic agree. With arguments, separate the claim from the evidence, and ask if the evidence is relevant and strong enough.
Paired passages test whether you can see where two authors agree and where they differ. Summarize each author's main view in a few words before you answer, so you can compare them clearly.

concepts.definition: A claim is the point the author wants you to accept. Evidence is the facts, data, or examples given to support it. Strong evidence is relevant, specific, and sufficient.
concepts.tip: Claim = what. Evidence = why you should believe it.

concepts.definition: Arguments can fail by using one example to make a big generalization, by confusing two things happening together with one causing the other, or by attacking a person instead of the idea.
concepts.tip: One story is not proof for everyone.

concepts.definition: Charts, tables, and graphs show data visually. Read the title, axis labels, legend, and units first, then find the exact value or trend the question asks about.
concepts.tip: Labels and units first, numbers second.

concepts.definition: Two short passages on one topic. Questions ask how the authors' views relate: they may agree, disagree, or one may add to or qualify the other.
concepts.tip: Write a few-word summary of each author's view before comparing.

concepts.definition: Some questions ask which new fact would make an argument stronger or weaker. The right answer directly affects the link between the evidence and the claim.
concepts.tip: Target the link between evidence and claim, not side details.

points: Check whether the evidence really supports the claim.
When two passages are paired, find where the authors agree and where they differ.
Read the labels and units on a chart before answering.
Two things happening together does not prove that one caused the other.

summary: This chapter covers the grammar rules tested in the usage questions of the Writing test. You will spot errors in subject-verb agreement, pronouns, verb tense, modifiers, word choice, and idioms. Some sentences are already correct, so part of the skill is knowing when to leave a sentence alone.

Two key skills are subject-verb agreement and pronoun agreement. Find the true subject even when a long phrase sits between it and the verb. Make sure each pronoun points clearly to one noun and matches it in number.

Verb tense should stay consistent unless the time really changes. Adjectives describe nouns, while adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. Idioms and commonly confused words, such as affect and effect, must be used the way standard English expects.

concepts.definition: A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Phrases between the subject and verb, like "of the students," do not change the subject.
concepts.tip: Cross out the middle phrase and read subject + verb together.

concepts.definition: A pronoun must match the noun it replaces in number and must clearly refer to one noun. In formal written English, words like each, everyone, and neither are treated as singular.
concepts.tip: If you can ask "who is 'they'?", the pronoun is unclear.

concepts.definition: Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) as subjects and object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) as objects, including after prepositions like between.
concepts.tip: "Between" is a preposition, so every pronoun after it takes the object form: "between you and me," never "between you and I."

concepts.definition: Keep the same tense throughout a sentence or passage unless the timing of the events really changes.
concepts.tip: Past stays past unless the clock moves.

concepts.definition: Adjectives describe nouns (a quick answer). Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs and often end in -ly (answered quickly).
concepts.tip: Describing an action? You usually need an adverb, often the -ly word (but fast, hard, and well are adverbs too).

concepts.definition: Standard English pairs some words with specific prepositions, such as "different from" and "capable of." Commonly confused pairs include affect/effect, its/it's, and their/there/they're.
concepts.tip: Read it aloud; wrong idioms usually sound off.

points: A verb must agree with its subject, even when other words come between them.
A pronoun must clearly refer to one noun and agree with it in number.
Some usage questions have no error, so do not force a change.
In formal written English, each, everyone, and neither are treated as singular and take singular verbs.
Use object pronouns after prepositions: between you and me.

summary: This chapter is about choosing the best way to write a sentence. You will fix run-ons and fragments, correct comma mistakes, make lists parallel, and move modifiers so they describe the right word. The best answer is grammatically correct, clear, and not wordy.

A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and must express a full thought. A fragment is missing one of these. A run-on joins two complete sentences without the right punctuation, and a comma splice joins them with only a comma.

Parallel structure means items in a list or comparison use the same grammatical form. A modifier should sit right next to the word it describes; when it does not, the sentence can say something silly. Among correct choices, the shorter one that keeps the full meaning is usually best.

concepts.definition: A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation. A comma splice joins them with only a comma. Fix with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word like and, but, or so.
concepts.tip: Two full sentences need a strong break: . or ; or , + and/but/so.

concepts.definition: A group of words punctuated as a sentence but missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought, such as "Because the bus was late."
concepts.tip: If it leaves you asking "and then what?", it is a fragment.

concepts.definition: Items in a list or comparison should share the same form: "reading, writing, and speaking," not "reading, writing, and to speak."
concepts.tip: Lists should match like a set of dishes.

concepts.definition: A describing phrase must be next to the word it describes. "Walking to school, the rain started" wrongly says the rain was walking.
concepts.tip: Ask who is doing the -ing action; that person must come right after the comma.

concepts.definition: A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences. A colon comes after a complete sentence to introduce a list, an explanation, or an example.
concepts.tip: Semicolon between two sentences: a full sentence on both sides. Colon: a full sentence before it.

concepts.definition: Avoid repeating the same idea or using extra words, as in "past history" or "due to the fact that." The shortest correct, clear choice is usually best.
concepts.tip: If two words say the same thing, cut one.

points: Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction (a colon also works when the second explains the first).
Items in a list should have the same grammatical form.
The best answer is correct, clear, and not wordy.
A modifier must sit next to the word it describes.
A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

compare.title: Fragment vs. run-on
rows: Add the missing subject, verb, or clause

summary: This chapter puts you in the role of an editor working on a short draft. You will choose transitions, combine sentences, decide whether to add or remove a sentence, and keep the focus and tone steady across the passage.

Transitions must match the real relationship between ideas, such as contrast, cause and effect, or adding an example. When combining sentences, the goal is a smooth sentence that keeps the original meaning without extra words.

For add-or-delete questions, check whether the sentence supports the paragraph's main point. A sentence that is interesting but off-topic should go. Finally, keep the same tone as the rest of the passage, so do not drop slang into a formal essay.

concepts.definition: Pick the transition that matches how two ideas relate: contrast (however), cause and effect (therefore), example (for instance), addition (furthermore), or time order (then).
concepts.tip: Read the sentence before and after, then name the relationship.

concepts.definition: Join two short sentences into one smooth sentence using a joining word, a relative clause (who, which, that), or a phrase, while keeping the meaning.
concepts.tip: Same meaning, fewer words, no new errors.

concepts.definition: A sentence belongs only if it supports the paragraph's main point. Remove sentences that drift to a different topic, even if they are true.
concepts.tip: Ask: "Does this help the main point?" If not, cut it.

concepts.definition: Revisions should match the passage's level of formality and point of view. Avoid slang in formal writing and avoid sudden shifts from he or she to you.
concepts.tip: The new sentence should sound like the same writer wrote it.

concepts.definition: Sentences and paragraphs should follow a clear order, such as time order or general-to-specific. Some questions ask where a sentence fits best.
concepts.tip: Look for clue words like first, then, this, or these that point back to earlier ideas.

points: A transition must match the relationship between the ideas.
Remove sentences that do not support the paragraph's main point.
Keep the tone and style of the rest of the passage.
When combining sentences, keep the original meaning and avoid extra words.

summary: This chapter covers the basics of doing research well. You will judge whether a source is credible and relevant, tell primary sources from secondary sources, and recognize the parts of a citation.

A credible source has a qualified author, is current enough for the topic, and shows where its information comes from. A relevant source actually addresses the research question. Both matter, because a trustworthy source on the wrong topic still does not help.

Primary sources are firsthand records, while secondary sources explain or interpret them. Citations let readers find a source again, so you should know the usual parts: author, title, publisher or journal, date, and pages.

concepts.definition: A trustworthy source with a qualified author or organization, up-to-date information for the topic, cited evidence, and no obvious bias or selling motive.
concepts.tip: Who wrote it, when, and how do they know?

concepts.definition: A source that directly addresses the specific research question. A credible source can still be useless if it covers a different topic, time, or group.
concepts.tip: Trustworthy is not enough; it must be on target.

concepts.definition: A primary source is a firsthand record, such as a diary, an original study, a speech, or a photograph. A secondary source explains or analyzes primary sources, such as a textbook or review article.
concepts.tip: Primary = was there. Secondary = writes about it later.

concepts.definition: A citation usually lists the author, the title of the work, the publisher or journal name, the publication date, and page numbers or a web address.
concepts.tip: Think "who, what, where, when" of the source.

concepts.definition: Using someone else's words or ideas without giving credit. Quotes and paraphrases both need a citation.
concepts.tip: Borrowed idea = cite it, even in your own words.

points: A credible source has a qualified author, is current enough, and shows its evidence.
A primary source is a firsthand record; a secondary source explains or interprets it.
Know the parts of a citation: author, title, publisher or journal, date, and pages.
A paraphrase still needs a citation.
Choose the source that answers the exact research question, not just a related one.

compare.title: Primary vs. secondary sources
rows: Firsthand record of an event or study
Diary, original research study, speech, photo

summary: This chapter is the largest part of the Math test. It covers integers, fractions, decimals, place value, ratios and proportions, percents, rates, and units of measurement. These skills also show up inside problems in every other chapter.

Fractions, decimals, and percents are three ways to write the same amount, so being able to switch between them quickly saves time. To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal and multiply.

Ratios compare two amounts, and a proportion says two ratios are equal, which you can solve by cross-multiplying. Rates, such as miles per hour, are ratios with different units. Always convert to the same unit before you add, subtract, or compare measurements.

concepts.definition: Change the percent to a decimal by dividing by 100, then multiply. For example, 15% of 80 = 0.15 × 80 = 12.
concepts.tip: "Of" means multiply.

concepts.definition: Percent change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.
concepts.tip: Always divide by the ORIGINAL amount.

concepts.definition: Two equal ratios, such as a/b = c/d. Solve by cross-multiplying: a × d = b × c, then divide to find the missing value.
concepts.tip: Keep the same units in the same positions on both sides.

concepts.definition: A rate compares two different units, like miles per hour. A unit rate gives the amount for one unit. Distance = rate × time.
concepts.tip: "Per" means divide.

concepts.definition: The same value in three forms: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom.
concepts.tip: Decimal to percent: move the point two places right.

concepts.definition: Multiply by a conversion factor equal to 1, such as 12 inches/1 foot or 60 minutes/1 hour, so the unwanted units cancel.
concepts.tip: Convert first, then calculate.

concepts.definition: Do parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.
concepts.tip: PEMDAS: Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally.

points: To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal and multiply.
Set up a proportion as two equal ratios and cross-multiply.
Convert units before you add or compare measurements.
For percent change, divide the change by the original value.
Multiplication and division are done left to right, as are addition and subtraction.

summary: This chapter covers the core tools of algebra. You will write and evaluate expressions, solve linear equations and inequalities, and turn word problems into equations you can solve.
An equation stays balanced only if you do the same operation to both sides. Work step by step to get the variable alone, then check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.

Inequalities are solved almost the same way, with one important difference: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign. In word problems, define the variable first and translate key words carefully.

concepts.definition: Replace each variable with its given value, then calculate using the order of operations. Use parentheses around negative numbers when substituting.
concepts.tip: Plug in with parentheses: x = −3 means (−3).

concepts.definition: Use inverse operations to get the variable alone, doing the same thing to both sides. Undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division.
concepts.tip: Keep the scale balanced.

concepts.definition: Solve like an equation, but flip the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number. Example: −2x > 6 becomes x < −3.
concepts.tip: Negative multiply or divide = flip the sign.

concepts.definition: Common key words: "is" means =, "of" means multiply, "more than" means add, "less than" means subtract (in reversed order: 5 less than x is x − 5).
concepts.tip: "Less than" flips the order.

concepts.definition: Multiply the number outside the parentheses by every term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
concepts.tip: Share with everyone inside the parentheses.

concepts.definition: Slope = (change in y) ÷ (change in x), or rise over run. In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is where the line crosses the y-axis.
concepts.tip: Rise over run.

points: Do the same operation to both sides of an equation.
When you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative number, flip the sign.
Check a solution by putting it back into the original equation.
"5 less than x" is written x − 5, not 5 − x.
Define what the variable stands for before writing an equation from a word problem.

summary: This chapter covers shapes and space. You will use angle facts, congruence and similarity, the Pythagorean theorem, and formulas for perimeter, area, and volume.

The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, and angles along a straight line also add up to 180 degrees. Similar figures have the same shape, so their angles are equal and their sides are proportional. Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size.

The Pythagorean theorem finds a missing side of a right triangle. Perimeter measures the distance around a shape, area measures the surface inside it in square units, and volume measures the space inside a solid in cubic units.

concepts.definition: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°. A right angle is 90°.
concepts.tip: Triangle and straight line: 180. Full turn: 360.

concepts.definition: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse, the longest side across from the right angle. A common example is 3, 4, 5.
concepts.tip: Only for right triangles; c is always the longest side.

concepts.definition: Similar figures have equal angles and proportional sides (same shape, any size). Congruent figures have equal angles and equal sides (same shape, same size).
concepts.tip: Similar = scaled copy. Congruent = exact copy.

concepts.definition: Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × height. Circle: π × r². Area is measured in square units.
concepts.tip: Triangle is half a rectangle.

concepts.definition: Perimeter is the sum of all side lengths. The distance around a circle is its circumference: 2 × π × r, or π × diameter.
concepts.tip: Perimeter = walk around the edge.

concepts.definition: Rectangular box: length × width × height. Cylinder: π × r² × height. Volume is measured in cubic units.
concepts.tip: Volume = area of the base × height.

points: The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Similar figures have equal angles and proportional sides.
Area uses square units; volume uses cubic units.
In a² + b² = c², c is the hypotenuse across from the right angle.
Radius is half the diameter; check which one the problem gives.

summary: This chapter is the second-largest part of the Math test. You will read tables and graphs, find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, and work out simple probabilities.

Reading data starts with the labels: check the title, the axes, the scale, and the units. Then the measures of center describe a typical value. The mean is the average, the median is the middle after ordering, and the mode is the most frequent value. The range shows the spread.

Outliers are values far from the rest. They pull the mean much more than the median, so the median often describes skewed data better. Probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the number of equally likely outcomes, giving a value from 0 to 1.

concepts.definition: The average: add all the values, then divide by how many values there are.
concepts.tip: Sum ÷ count.

concepts.definition: The middle value after putting the data in order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
concepts.tip: Order first, then find the middle.

concepts.definition: The mode is the value that appears most often; a set can have no mode or more than one. The range is the largest value minus the smallest value.
concepts.tip: Mode = most. Range = max − min.

concepts.definition: A value much higher or lower than the rest of the data. Outliers change the mean much more than the median or mode.
concepts.tip: One giant salary raises the average but barely moves the middle.

concepts.definition: P(event) = number of favorable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. Probability is between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
concepts.tip: What you want ÷ everything that can happen.

concepts.definition: When one event does not affect the other, the probability that both happen is P(A) × P(B). Example: two coin flips both heads = ½ × ½ = ¼.
concepts.tip: "And" with independent events means multiply.

concepts.definition: Check the title, axis labels, scale, and units before reading values. Bar graphs compare categories, line graphs show change over time, and circle graphs show parts of a whole.
concepts.tip: Watch the scale: it may not start at zero or count by ones.

points: The median is the middle value after the data are put in order.
An outlier changes the mean much more than the median.
Probability = favorable outcomes divided by all equally likely outcomes.
Range is the largest value minus the smallest value.
Check a graph's scale before reading values from it.

compare.title: Mean vs. median vs. mode
rows: Add all values, divide by the count
